## [Scott Colom Wins Stunning Victory, Becomes Mississippi's First Black Senator Since Reconstruction](http://www.democracynow.org/2026/11/12/scott_colom_victory_speech)

via Democracy Now · 2026-11-12

Democrat Scott Colom has made history as Mississippi’s first Democratic senator since 1982 — and its first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Colom’s victory brings the incoming Senate Democratic caucus to 55. Colom gave his victory speech on Wednesday at the historically Black Tougaloo College, just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.

“There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith,” said Colom. “There are so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers.”

## ["Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon](http://www.democracynow.org/2026/11/11/birds_of_war)

via Democracy Now · 2026-11-11

We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary _Birds of War_, which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC, and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence.

The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions.

“Without our journalistic relationship, \[we\] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.”

_Birds of War_ premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

## ["American Scoundrel": From Roy Cohn to Stephen Miller, "McCarthyism Lives On," Says Author Kai Bird](http://www.democracynow.org/2026/11/11/kai_bird_american_scoundrel)

via Democracy Now · 2026-11-11

We speak with historian Kai Bird about _American Scoundrel_, a new biography of the notorious political fixer Roy Cohn, who rose to fame as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy during the senator’s anti-communist campaign, served as a lawyer for the New York mob, and was an influential voice in Republican circles until his death from AIDS-related complications in 1986. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s.

Facing political setbacks during his first term as president, Trump reportedly asked, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Bird, who co-authored _American Scoundrel_ with his wife Susan Goldmark, says Trump may have found his Cohn in Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation policies whom Trump just elevated to chief of staff.

“It’s not really a surprise that, cornered and wounded by the recent election results, he reaches out and pulls up Stephen Miller, who’s very similar in his willingness to go on the offensive and never back down, and to say outrageous things to try to change the narrative,” says Bird.

Shin was named chairman of the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) following consultations among members at the BIS Global Economy Meeting (GEM), according to the BOK. His three-year term began on Nov. 1. The CPMI is an international standards-setting body dedicated to enhancing the stability and efficiency of payment systems and financial market infrastructure. It also serves as a key consultative body among central banks under the BIS GEM. Shin is the first non-American and non-European to chair the CPMI since the committee was established in 1990 as the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems. With Shin's appointment, the BOK is expected to strengthen its leadership in the global financial community by taking a leading role in establishing international standards for payment and settlement systems.

## ["A Crackdown on All Independent Voices": Egypt Shutters News Outlets, Prosecutes Editor Lina Attalah](http://www.democracynow.org/2026/11/9/egypt_mada_masr_lina_attalah)

via Democracy Now · 2026-11-09

Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet _Mada Masr_, faces a criminal trial this week on charges of “spreading false information,” just two weeks after being convicted of operating an unlicensed website and fined more than $50,000. A judge also ordered the publication to be shut down. The cases are part of a broader crackdown on independent Egyptian media under the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, including the arrest of the entire newsroom of another outlet, _Matsadaash_. More than 100 organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and prosecutions and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges.

“Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems,” Attalah told _Democracy Now!_ in an interview Friday. “We need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms.”

Attalah says she and _Mada Masr_ will appeal the ruling to shut them down, hoping to “use this crisis” as a way to fight censorship in Egypt and expand the space for independent reporting.

## [POSCO union votes down tentative wage deal](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/companies/20261107/posco-union-votes-down-tentative-wage-deal?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-07

Unionized workers at Korean steelmaker POSCO on Saturday voted down a tentative wage agreement reached with management that includes a 2.6 percent increase in base pay, union officials said. The vote showed 51.69 percent of the unionized workers opposed the wage agreement, while 48.31 percent approved it, according to the union. The tentative wage deal includes a 2.6 percent hike in base pay, a one-off payment of 6 million won ($4,500) and improved benefits. The union had initially demanded a 7.1 percent increase in base pay, a performance bonus equivalent to 600 percent of base pay, 50 company shares per worker and a holiday bonus equivalent to 200 percent of base pay. "We will probably need to open renegotiations as there were many opposing votes," a union official said. The union and management reached a tentative wage agreement on Oct. 30 after holding about 30 rounds of talks since June. Unionized POSCO workers staged two rounds of partial strikes in September to demand higher wages and bonuses.

SEYMEN, Turkey — In the countryside west of Istanbul, trucks line up to empty mixed household waste from the city of 16 million people onto a vast landscape of decomposing rubbish, where landfill gas is captured to generate electricity at a nearby plant. But far above the seagulls circling the waste, satellites detect what the plant has failed to capture: methane escaping at a rate that ranks it among the world’s largest recorded landfill emitters. Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya from Nov. 9–20 and has made methane reduction a priority for the climate summit. Methane is the biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide (CO2) and is over 80 times more potent than CO2 in its first 20 years in the air. Sharp cuts could therefore slow warming relatively quickly. Turkey's waste sector illustrates both the potential and the difficulty of achieving rapid cuts. The country is the world's fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste behind China, the United States, Russia and Brazil, according to data from nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE. BRUSSELS — The European Union on Friday announced tighter health safety rules for baby formula following a contamination scandal involving cereulide, a toxin which can cause severe vomiting in newborns. The 27 member states approved the introduction of a "permanent food safety criterion for cereulide in infant formula", the European Commission said in a statement. In December 2025 food giant Nestle recalled dozens of infant formula batches in around 60 countries over the potential presence of the toxin. Similar recalls by manufacturers including Danone and Lactalis followed, up to April 2026. The EU said the contamination originated from the use of a Chinese-imported ingredient, an oil containing arachidonic acid. The presence of cereulide in products resulted from "deficiencies in the production process," the EU Commission's statement said. "Member states have approved strict maximum safety limits for the presence of the toxin in dried and liquid products."

If elected, Colom would be the first Democrat to win the state in 40 years and the first African American since 1875, during the Reconstruction era. Colom, the former district attorney for northeast Mississippi, made the issue of affordability central to his campaign. He has sharply criticized national Democrats for writing off Mississippi and failing to invest in his campaign early on.

“The entire country shifted left. But when you look at it regionally, the biggest shifts took place in the South — Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Louisiana,” says Cliff Albright, executive director of Black Voters Matter. That “wave of energy” was “largely led by Black voters who were most under attack with the mid-decade racial gerrymandering that was taking place. It clearly backfired, and all it did was to wake up a sleeping giant.”

“Without the extreme gerrymandering, without the extreme voter restrictions that have been seen throughout the South, \[the\] wave would have been even bigger,” adds Chris Kromm, executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies. “There’s a real opportunity for engaging more voters and really pushing the region in a more progressive direction.”

Canada classifies trading profits as either capital gains or business income. For capital gains, only half the profit is included in taxable income. The government is pushing to expand the definition of stalking to include tracking victims' locations and monitoring their social media activity, among other actions, as part of efforts to swiftly separate perpetrators from victims, the justice ministry said Tuesday. The ministry said an amendment to the Act on Punishment of Crime of Stalking was proposed Oct. 26 to make nine types of controlling behavior within a relationship criminal offenses. ## [Election Protection: NAACP on Voter Suppression & Deployment of Federal Poll Monitors](http://www.democracynow.org/2026/11/3/voting_rights_election_protection)

via Democracy Now · 2026-11-03

As President Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections, signaling his intentions to challenge results unfavorable to Republicans, we go to Washington, D.C., where a federal judge ruled Monday night that the Department of Justice can deploy election monitors to polling sites across the country, as long as they are not law enforcement officers with the power to make arrests. “In some respects, this is a victory for voters. Every voter in our country deserves to be able to cast a ballot today, free from intimidation,” says Kristen Clarke of the NAACP, which sued to challenge the DOJ’s plans to deploy ICE agents and other armed officers to the polls.

The NAACP was also part of a coalition that intervened when the Trump administration attempted to force California to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleged were sent incorrectly to noncitizens. “This was a baseless, error-prone, shoddy 11th-hour attempt to hijack the election in California, plain and simple, and it’s now been rejected by four courts,” Clarke says. The administration’s attacks on voters “are not bearing fruit,” she adds. “We anticipate and are ready for anything that they may throw our way.”

## [Japan launches new national agency to deal with disasters](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/world/20261102/japan-launches-new-national-agency-to-deal-with-disasters?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-02

TOKYO — Japan on Monday launched a new national agency focused on disaster management to improve the country's preparedness if there's a megaquake along the Pacific coast or in Tokyo, or an eruption of Mount Fuji. More than 350 workers at the National Disaster Management Agency will oversee preparedness, emergency response and reconstruction efforts. The agency was not created in anticipation of any specific calamity, but to address concerns about whether the nation is prepared for a crisis on the scale of the 2011 quake and tsunami in northern Japan, which killed nearly 20,000 people, and the subsequent Fukushima nuclear disaster. Japan, which lies along the Pacific "Ring of Fire,” is one of the most disaster-prone countries but it has never had an agency dedicated to the task. “As the command center of disaster response, we will do everything to strengthen our preparedness to protect people's lives and properties ... and aim to become the world's most prepared,” Reconstruction Minister Goshi Hosono said. He will manage the agency headed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi

## ["Princes and Thieves" Author Matthew Cole on Jared Kushner & the "Secret Plot to Remake Middle East"](http://www.democracynow.org/2026/11/2/matthew_cole_jared_kushner_book)

via Democracy Now · 2026-11-02

_Vanity Fair_ recently published an [excerpt](https://www.vanityfair.com/story/jared-kushner-hacked-phone-secret-negotiations) from longtime investigative reporter Matthew Cole’s new book, _Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East_.

The excerpt alleged that during President Trump’s first term, Saudi and Emirati leaders secretly put at least $2 billion into bank accounts and gave access to Kushner. At the time, Jared Kushner was serving as senior adviser to President Trump, his father-in-law. He is now Trump’s special envoy. Kushner’s lawyers responded by demanding that _Vanity Fair_ retract the article and threatening legal action against the book publisher, Simon & Schuster.

Jared Kushner denied the report, saying, “The allegations made by this author are completely insane, categorically false, and never happened. We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” His lawyers say no such bank accounts existed and that the allegations are unsupported by the verifiable evidence.

In an extended interview with _Democracy Now!_, author Matthew Cole stood by his reporting. “This book is a result of more than 50 sources. There was an enormous amount of fact-checking and legal vetting that went into this book,” says Cole. “There’s plenty of information and reporting in the book that lets us establish and understand that there was … an unholy alliance between Jared Kushner and the leader of the UAE, the leader of Saudi Arabia and, at the time, Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel.”

On Friday, Congressmember Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called on Kushner to recuse himself from Middle East and Ukraine negotiations and to produce a “comprehensive list of bank accounts or other financial instruments” that he had access to during his time in government.

The women about to become middle and high school students did not dress or look like other students. They wore hanbok, traditional Korean clothing, instead of uniforms, and not one of them looked like typical teenagers worn down by a nagging parent. Among them was 77-year-old Lee Bok-gae, who was entering middle school that morning — an adult learner, one of the women who lost their chance at school due to financial difficulties and gender inequality in education. Born the eldest of seven children, studying became an elusive dream, as she had to work while caring for her younger siblings. That same day, her granddaughter became a middle school student, too. ## [Pianist Lim Dong-hyek to perform Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 2 in Seoul](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/entertainment/20261031/pianist-lim-dong-hyek-to-perform-rachmaninoffs-piano-concerto-no-2-in-seoul?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-10-31

Pianist Lim Dong-hyek will perform one of the most beloved works in the piano repertoire when he performs Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 2 under the baton of creative conductor Adriel Kim this November. Having scaled back his recent concert appearances, Lim will perform the concerto for the first time in four years, making the occasion a particularly meaningful encounter with audiences. The concert marks the first collaboration between Lim and Orchestra The Original. Audiences will be watching to see how Lim’s delicate touch and Kim’s meticulous conducting combine to create a distinctive musical dialogue. At the heart of the program is Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 2.
